review.Summary: The paper introduces StyleAR, a method for enabling multimodal autoregressive (AR) models to perform style-aligned text-to-image generation. The key challenge addressed is the scarcity of text-image-to-image triplet data required for instruction-following tuning of AR models. The authors propose: (1) a data curation strategy that constructs binary prompt-stylized-image data (dropping the reference style image) using a diffusion model as a data generator, (2) mixing these stylized images with raw images from large-scale datasets at a 3:1 ratio during training, (3) a CLIP image encoder with perceiver resampler to convert input images into style tokens compatible with AR model token space, and (4) a style-enhanced token technique using SAM-based feature subtraction and Gaussian noise injection to prevent content leakage. The method also incorporates DPO post-training. Experiments compare against several diffusion-based baselines (InstantStyle, IP-Adapter, StyleAligned, StyleCrafter, StyleShot) on prompt adherence (CLIP-T) and style consistency (CLIP-I, DINO), with ablations on dataset composition, style-enhanced tokens, and DPO, plus a user study.
Strengths: Novel approach to a relatively unexplored problem: enabling AR models for style-aligned generation, which is currently dominated by diffusion-based methods
Practical solution to the triplet data scarcity problem by using binary data with a clever data curation strategy
The style-enhanced token technique (SAM + Gaussian noise) is an interesting and effective approach to address content leakage
Comprehensive evaluation including quantitative metrics, qualitative comparisons, ablations, and user study
Retains additional capabilities of the base AR model (e.g., structural control) which is demonstrated qualitatively
Clear figures and tables that effectively illustrate the method and results
Weaknesses: Limited evaluation scope: only 10 style images and 20 prompts used for evaluation, which may not be sufficiently representative or diverse
The paper does not achieve the highest score on any single quantitative metric (second in CLIP-T, CLIP-I, and DINO), yet claims state-of-the-art performance - this claim needs more justification
The explanation that IP-Adapter's high CLIP-I/DINO scores are due to content leakage is plausible but not rigorously validated with controlled experiments

The data curation relies on a diffusion model (InstantStyle) for generating stylized training data, which partially contradicts the motivation of avoiding diffusion model capability limits, though the binary formulation does mitigate this
The paper could provide more analysis on why the 3:1 stylized-to-raw ratio is optimal and how sensitive the method is to this hyperparameter
Some technical details are unclear, such as the exact implementation of the perceiver resampler and how it integrates with the AR model's token space
No comparison with other AR-based approaches (though the paper notes this is the first work in this area, it would strengthen the paper to show why other AR methods fail)
Questions: The paper claims state-of-the-art performance but achieves second place on all three quantitative metrics. How do you justify this claim? Could you provide statistical significance tests (e.g., confidence intervals) for the differences between methods?
How sensitive is the method to the number of style tokens (M=16)? Have you experimented with different values?
What is the impact of the Gaussian noise strength (gamma) on the trade-off between style consistency and prompt adherence? Is there a sweet spot?
The training uses 16,000 stylized images from 80 styles. How does performance scale with more styles or more images per style? Is there a saturation point?
Could you elaborate on why the 3:1 ratio is optimal? What happens at ratios between 1:3 and 1:6?
In the user study, how many participants were involved and what was the inter-rater reliability?
Have you tested StyleAR on styles that are very different from those in the training set (e.g., 3D render, pixel art, watercolor)? How does generalization work?
The paper mentions 'content leakage' as a common issue. Could you provide a more formal definition or metric to quantify content leakage?
How does the inference-time use of SAM affect computational cost compared to training-time? Is SAM applied to every reference image at inference?
Limitations: The evaluation is limited to 10 styles and 20 prompts, which may not capture the full diversity of style-aligned generation scenarios
The method still depends on a diffusion model for generating stylized training data, which could introduce biases from the diffusion model
The paper does not address potential negative societal impacts, such as the potential misuse of style imitation for copyright infringement or creating misleading content
The computational cost of the method (training on top of Lumina-mGPT, plus SAM inference at test time) is not discussed
The paper only demonstrates results on one base AR model (Lumina-mGPT); generalizability to other AR models is unclear

This paper proposes StyleAR, a method for enabling autoregressive (AR) models to perform style-aligned text-to-image generation using binary text-image data instead of the more challenging triplet data. The key contributions include: (1) a data curation strategy that drops the reference style image and uses only prompt-stylized image pairs generated by a diffusion model, (2) mixing raw and stylized images at a 3:1 ratio for training, (3) a CLIP image encoder with perceiver resampler to convert image inputs into style tokens, and (4) a style-enhanced token technique using SAM and Gaussian noise injection to prevent content leakage. They also apply DPO post-training.

The paper is technically interesting as it addresses a novel problem (AR models for style-aligned generation) and proposes a practical solution to the data scarcity issue. The experiments are reasonably thorough with comparisons to several diffusion-based baselines, ablations on dataset composition and module designs, and a user study.

However, there are several concerns:
1. The evaluation is limited in scope - only 10 styles and 20 prompts, which may not be representative. The results show only marginal improvements over baselines in some metrics.
2. The claim of "state-of-the-art" is questionable since they don't achieve the highest scores on any single metric (they're second in CLIP-T, CLIP-I, and DINO).
3. The content leakage explanation for IP-Adapter's high CLIP-I/DINO scores is plausible but not rigorously validated.
4. The method relies on a diffusion model (InstantStyle) for data generation, which somewhat contradicts their goal of avoiding the "upper bound" of diffusion models - though they argue the binary data formulation avoids this.
5. The paper has some clarity issues, particularly in the methodology section where the training and inference formulations could be clearer.
6. The ablation study on dataset composition shows interesting trade-offs, but the paper could provide more analysis on why the 3:1 ratio is optimal.

The paper is well-written overall with clear figures and tables. The work is original in its approach to using binary data for AR-based style generation. The technical quality is good, though the evaluation could be more comprehensive.

I would rate this as a borderline accept - the idea is novel and the results are promising, but the evaluation is somewhat limited and the claimed superiority is not fully demonstrated.

review.Summary: The paper introduces StyleAR, the first framework enabling multimodal autoregressive (AR) models to perform style-aligned text-to-image generation. The authors propose a novel data curation method that converts the challenging text-image-to-image triplet data requirement into a simpler binary text-image data setup by generating stylized images with diffusion models (InstantStyle) and using only the prompt and stylized image for training. To enable binary data training, they integrate a CLIP image encoder with a perceiver resampler to convert images into style tokens, and introduce a style-enhanced token technique combining SAM-based feature subtraction and Gaussian noise injection to prevent content leakage. They also employ a mixed training strategy combining stylized and raw images (1:3 ratio) and DPO post-training. Extensive experiments including qualitative comparisons, quantitative metrics (CLIP-T, CLIP-I, DINO), and user studies demonstrate competitive performance against diffusion-based baselines like InstantStyle, IP-Adapter, StyleAligned, StyleCrafter, and StyleShot.
Strengths: Novel problem formulation: First work to tackle style-aligned text-to-image generation with autoregressive models, which is an underexplored area compared to diffusion-based approaches.
Innovative data curation strategy: Using binary text-image data instead of triplet data avoids the upper bound limitation of diffusion-based data generators and enables easier data scaling.

Well-designed style-enhanced tokens technique: The combination of SAM-based feature subtraction and Gaussian noise injection effectively addresses content leakage, a known challenge in style transfer.

Comprehensive experimental validation: Includes qualitative comparisons, quantitative metrics, user studies, and thorough ablation studies for dataset composition, style-enhanced tokens, and DPO post-training.
Demonstrated extensibility: Shows the method can integrate additional conditions (e.g., depth maps) while maintaining style consistency and quality.
Weaknesses: Limited evaluation scale: Only 10 reference styles, 20 prompts, and 800 generated images for evaluation, which may not sufficiently demonstrate generalization across diverse styles and prompts.
Fairness of comparisons: Baseline methods use different base architectures (SD1.5 for StyleShot, SDXL for others), and the paper doesn't control for base model quality differences.

Reliance on diffusion for data generation: The stylized training data is generated using InstantStyle (a diffusion method), which partially contradicts the motivation of avoiding diffusion model limitations.

Marginal quantitative improvements: StyleAR doesn't achieve the best score on any single metric (CLIP-T, CLIP-I, DINO), and the justification for IP-Adapter's inflated style metrics due to content leakage, while plausible, is not rigorously quantified.

Insufficient details on DPO implementation: The paper mentions using a VLM for preference selection but doesn't specify which VLM, how many preference pairs were used, or the training hyperparameters for DPO.
Lack of computational cost comparison: No information on training/inference time or resource requirements compared to diffusion baselines.
Limited user study information: Number of participants, evaluation protocol, and statistical significance are not reported.
Questions: How does the choice of sampling 10% of raw image data per epoch affect training dynamics? What is the exact number of training steps and epochs used?
Can you provide more details on the DPO post-training? Which specific VLM was used for preference scoring, how many preference pairs were constructed, and what were the DPO training hyperparameters?
What is the computational cost comparison (training time, inference speed, GPU memory) between StyleAR and the diffusion baselines?
How sensitive is the method to the number of style tokens (M=16)? Have you experimented with different values?
What is the rationale for the specific residual ratio α in Equation 2? Is it fixed or tuned?
How would StyleAR perform with more diverse and challenging styles beyond the 80 used in training? Have you tested with styles not in the training set?
Could you elaborate on the content leakage issue in IP-Adapter? Have you quantified the semantic similarity between generated images and reference style images to support this claim?
How does the 1:3 stylized-to-raw ratio scale with larger datasets? Would this ratio need adjustment with more data?
Limitations: The current implementation requires depth map extraction for content control rather than directly accepting a content image input, limiting the flexibility for certain style transfer scenarios.
The training data is limited to 80 styles, which may not capture the full diversity of artistic styles in real-world applications.
The method's performance heavily depends on the quality of the diffusion-based data generator (InstantStyle) for creating stylized training images.
Potential negative societal impact: The method could be misused to generate images in copyrighted artistic styles without permission, raising concerns about artistic intellectual property rights.
The evaluation is limited to English prompts and Western-centric styles, potentially limiting generalizability to other cultural contexts.
